passages.t: From the Sheep Gate around to the Dung Gate
passages.happening:
The chapter goes around the wall, section by section, and names who rebuilt each part. It begins with the high priest. ‘At the Sheep Gate, Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests began rebuilding. They dedicated it and installed its doors’ (verse 1).

Then come the men of Jericho, the sons of Hassenaah, who rebuilt the Fish Gate and set its beams, doors, bolts and bars (verse 3), and family after family. ‘Next to him, the Tekoites made repairs, but their nobles did not put their shoulders to the work under their supervisors’ (verse 5).

The list goes on: men of Gibeon and Mizpah, a goldsmith and the son of a perfumer (verse 8), district rulers, and ‘Shallum son of Hallohesh, ruler of the other half-district of Jerusalem’, who made repairs ‘with the help of his daughters’ (verse 12). The Valley Gate and the Dung Gate are rebuilt and given new doors, bolts and bars (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 2 ended with the people agreeing to start rebuilding. Chapter 3 pauses the story to name the people who did it. The wall was not Nehemiah's achievement alone but the work of the whole community, organized section by section.

The circuit starts at the Sheep Gate near the temple, on the north, and moves west and south. Ancient city gates were more than openings: they were towers with heavy wooden doors, bolts and bars, and they served as markets and courts. Several are named for what passed through them. The Sheep Gate was probably where animals for sacrifice came in. The Fish Gate may have been where fish were sold, and the Dung Gate led to the city's rubbish dump.

The work was organized by household and by town. Men came from Jericho, Gibeon, Mizpah and Tekoa, and district rulers led work parties. That gives a glimpse of how the Persian province of Judah was run.

Two notes stand out. Shallum worked with his daughters, which is unusual in an ancient building list; perhaps he had no sons, or their work was too notable to leave out. And the nobles of Tekoa would not bend their necks to the work, an elite unwilling to do manual labor or to take orders from Nehemiah's supervisors. They are the only ones the list blames.

The Broad Wall of verse 8 may be connected with a massive wall from the late eighth century BC that the archaeologist Nahman Avigad uncovered in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter in the 1970s, and named after this verse. Whether Nehemiah's builders used that line is debated.
passages.later:
The Sheep Gate was still there in the Gospels: ‘Now there is in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate a pool with five covered colonnades, which in Hebrew is called Bethesda’ (John 5:2).

The high priest Eliashib who began the work was the grandson of Jeshua, the priest of the first return: ‘Jeshua was the father of Joiakim, Joiakim was the father of Eliashib’ (Nehemiah 12:10).
passages.asks: The nobles of Tekoa would not put their shoulders to the work, and their own townspeople built two sections. Ask whether you have ever thought some work was beneath you. And ask what it would mean to work beside others, as Shallum's daughters did, whether or not anyone expected it of you.

passages.t: Up the eastern side and back to the Sheep Gate
passages.happening:
The Fountain Gate is rebuilt by the ruler of the district of Mizpah, who also repairs the wall of the Pool of Shelah ‘near the king’s garden, as far as the stairs that descend from the City of David’ (verse 15). The list moves north along the eastern side, past the tombs of David, the artificial pool, the House of the Mighty and the house of the high priest, with Levites, priests and men from the towns each at their section (verses 16-25).

‘And the temple servants living on the hill of Ophel made repairs opposite the Water Gate toward the east and the tower that juts out’ (verse 26). The Tekoites, whose nobles had refused, repair a second section (verse 27). ‘Above the Horse Gate, each of the priests made repairs in front of his own house’ (verse 28).

And the circuit closes where it began: ‘between the upper room above the corner and the Sheep Gate, the goldsmiths and merchants made repairs’ (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The first half of the list is arranged by gates. This second half, along the eastern side, is arranged by houses, towers and landmarks, and many people repair the stretch in front of their own homes. That was practical: people defended what was nearest them. It also gave every family a share in the whole.

Most scholars think Nehemiah's Jerusalem was much smaller than the city before the exile. It covered the temple mount and the narrow ridge of the old City of David, not the broader western hill the later kings had enclosed.

The word for repaired is chazaq, to be strong or to strengthen, and it comes about thirty-five times in the chapter. As the wall is made strong, so are the people. And the phrase next to them is, in Hebrew, at their hand: workers standing side by side, each at the hand of the next, all along the wall.

Several names connect with the rest of the book. Meremoth son of Uriah, who had received Ezra's treasure (Ezra 8:33), repairs two sections. Meshullam son of Berechiah, who works here, will later give his daughter in marriage to Tobiah's son. The Nehemiah son of Azbuk in verse 16 is a different man from the governor.
passages.later:
Meremoth the priest had received the treasure Ezra brought: ‘we weighed out the silver and gold and sacred articles into the hand of Meremoth son of Uriah, the priest’ (Ezra 8:33).

The circuit ends at the gates where it began, and the wall will be dedicated with two choirs walking on top of it (Nehemiah 12:31-40).
passages.asks: The chapter records names, not speeches: ordinary people repairing the part of the wall in front of their own houses. Ask what the section in front of your house is, the part of God's work nearest to you. And ask whose quiet work around you deserves to be named.
